items.item: Insertion sort's work is proportional to how far from sorted the input already is, not just its size
Insertion sort makes zero moves on already-sorted input, only n-1 comparisons
Selection sort's comparison count never changes no matter how sorted the input already is
Selection sort bounds its writes to at most one per position, which is why it's chosen when writes are expensive (e.g. flash memory)
Bubble sort with an early-exit check is technically adaptive but still loses to insertion sort on the same input

items.item: A sort can be stable without being in place, and in place without being stable — the four combinations aren't all equally easy to achieve together
A hybrid sort's insertion-sort fallback threshold is chosen because small-input overhead (recursion, function calls) dominates asymptotic savings at that size

items.item: A sorting network is still bound by the same comparison-model lower bound as any other comparison sort, since it never skips a comparison based on the data
Meeting the lower bound exactly at one small input size doesn't mean an algorithm is optimal at every size
The same four input-shape questions (random, sorted, reversed, duplicates) that matter for insertion sort reappear for every later sort in this chapter
